title: Choose the visual world
question: The roll assigned the Harbor Chart. Keep it, take an alternate, or re-roll.

options.label: Harbor Chart
options.lineage: NOAA nautical charts of Charlotte Harbor, the water next to Babcock Ranch
options.thesis: The company drawn as a living navigation chart: the lab is home port, each product a charted light you can steer to.
options.viewport: A full-bleed chart drawn live: depth contours shift under the cursor like a tide; a plotted course runs from home port to three product lights, each with a real link.
options.risk: Can read as a maritime theme park if the chart conventions are pasted on rather than used to navigate.

raised.raise: Status is a chart mark, not a color: Live is a lit light, Waitlist an unlit buoy, In Development marked PA (position approximate).
Rank by type style, not size: water names italic, land names upright, product names in spaced caps, as real charts do.
The hero wakes in sequence along one course line: each light switches on in turn as the course reaches it.
Every region is labeled literally, chart-legend style, so finding things is just reading.
Open water stays open: one move per viewport and real negative space around the course.

options.label: Sunprint
options.lineage: Cyanotype sun prints, the kitchen-table science of a solar-powered town
options.thesis: Everything the lab makes, exposed onto Prussian-blue paper by the Florida sun.
options.viewport: A deep-blue sheet where the cursor is the sun: moving it develops the print, revealing the three products as white silhouettes.
options.risk: Close to the craft-paper look many studio sites ship; it relies on the exposure effect to stand apart.

options.label: Claim and Proof
options.lineage: Monochrome product marketing, translated to one blue
options.thesis: Every sentence about the lab is followed by a product screen that proves it.
options.viewport: Short headline on near-white, then Ripple Pool's real screen at large scale with its play link.
options.case: Wins on product clarity, loses on audience identification: it could be any studio.
options.risk: Edges toward the generic startup look you asked to avoid.

options.label: Cutting Bench Rail
options.thesis: Products strung as frames along a perforated rail.
options.viewport: A frame rail across the page, one product per frame.
options.case: Players and Hunchwell prospects don't recognize film editing, and its orange fights the blue brief.
options.kept: Status as a mark, not a color.

options.label: Emission Line Rail
options.thesis: Everything registered against one calibrated rail.
options.viewport: A spectrum rail with one plate open.
options.case: Too cold and abstract for a family lab; product pitches get lost in the hairlines.
options.kept: Rank by type style and ink, not by size.

options.label: Garden Vistas
options.thesis: A choreographed axis with hidden rooms.
options.viewport: An axial vista down to three bosquets.
options.case: Royal grandeur is the opposite of a small family lab, and it isn't blue.

options.label: Quoted Streetwear
options.thesis: Every zone named in straight quotes.
options.case: Its irony clashes with the warm, plain voice and the calm games.
options.kept: Literal labels: finding things is just reading.

options.label: Fashion Flagship
options.thesis: Slow full-bleed images between vast white space.
options.viewport: One huge word and a single image.
options.case: Feels too luxury and too cold for a family lab; there's no photography to carry it.
options.kept: Real negative space, one move per viewport.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: An indie studio home page, done well: wordmark, short headline, three product cards with screenshots.
canonCard.viewport: Headline and subline at left, products in a row of three below.
canonCard.risk: Looks like every other studio by design.
